Use:

> library(devtools)
> dev_mode(TRUE)
> install.packages(...)

This will install your packages in a temporary development environment.  You have fine grained control - you can specify a path as an argument to dev_mode()

Good luck with your project.

Andrie

Here’s the way an rpm install can be done by a non-root user:

Unpack the installation tarball to find the rpm.

rpm --initdb --dbpath $HOME/localrpmdb

export MY_RPM_DBPATH=$HOME/localrpmdb && \

    rpm --dbpath $MY_RPM_DBPATH --prefix $HOME \

    --nodeps -i RRO-*.x86_64.rpm

For a Debian package manager, use this:

 dpkg -i --force-not-root --root=$HOME package.deb

Let me know how that goes for you.

Hi, Jason

At a guess, you are using a 4-core machine with hyperthreading.

The Intel MKL only works on real cores, not the hyperthreading, so the maximum in your case would be 4 cores.

Hyperthreading means that the same physical core acts to run 2 processes at the same time Thus, for high performance computing, you can not get any additional benefit from the hyperthreading.

I hope this helps.

Andrie

Try this on the machine with RRO 3.2.2 installed on it:

Then try reinstalling the rJava package.

Hi Jason,

Perhaps this will answer your question.  We found the following on a Mathematica Google Group site:

>
> The end result is that a Bulldozer core is "worth" about half a Sandy
>
> Bridge core, clock for clock, especially in floating-point workloads since
>
> a single FP unit is shared between two of what AMD calls cores (indeed,
>
> many have said that AMD's "8 core" processors are more correctly referred
>
> to as genuinely having 4 cores due to much shared apparatus, but for
>
> marketing reasons, AMD is obviously not buying that argument).

Since MKL is all about floating point computations, if there are only 4 FP units, it is possible that MKL is seeing 4 cores where AMD is claiming 8…

Hi Rajeev,

RRO doesn't have a explicit dependency on Java itself. RRO will only install those system libraries
that are a dependency required for base R itself. That is why we don't install libicu by default.

Hi Yifan,

On Ubuntu it is necessary to set an additional Rstudio environment variable.

Please try the following(this worked for me):
1). From a Linux shell prompt, type:
 %export RSTUDIO_WHICH_R=/usr/bin/R

2). Make sure that a link '/usr/bin/R' exists in your install and points to the following:
 /usr//lib64/RRO-3.2.2/R-3.2.2/lib/R/bin/R

3). Make sure that port 8787 is open on your system.

4). Open a web browser and point it to:
 http://:<your.machine.ip.address>:8787 <http://:%3Cyour.machine.ip.address%3E:8787>
This should open Rstudio with a login prompt.

5). If you want to permanently set the environment variable, 'RSTUDIO_WHICH_R' add it to your .bash_profile file in your user home directory.

Stephen Weller

messages.subject_clean: RRO-3.2.2 broke RStudio Server for me
messages.body_plain:
As reported on Github <https://github.com/RevolutionAnalytics/RRO/issues/241>, it may be related to the following:

Line 4 in /usr/lib64/RRO-3.2.2/R-3.2.2/lib64/R/bin/R determines R_HOME_DIR based on readlink /proc/$$/fd/255. Since this command is implementation-dependent, it does not work the same way across each environment. Some users have had success by updating line 4 to use the absolute path to R such as:
R_HOME_DIR=/usr/lib64/RRO-3.2.2/R-3.2.2/lib64/R
R_HOME_DIR=/usr/lib64/RRO-3.2.2/R-3.2.2/lib/R

The actual path depends on your environment or distribution. Hope this helps.

Thanks,
Josée
